Epilogue: Primary Process Revisited

Lester Lenoff LCSWIssue Editor

Lester Lenoff

Lester Lenoff   Contact Lester Lenoff, LCSW lstrlenoff@gmail.com 150 East 57th Street, Apt. 24AB, New York, NY 10022.

We might summarize Freud’s radical contribution as the recognition, in the words of a recent Nobel Laureate, “something is happening here but you don’t know what it is” (Dylan, 1965, side 1, track 5). The authors and articles in this issue propose variations on that something that can clarify a reader’s thinking while offering a platform for further exploration.

Linda Brakel concludes that psychoanalytic general theory of primary process provides two key contributions, “the key roles of meaningful unconscious processes and that of the a-rational primary processes throughout mental life” (p. 183). In the course of fulfilling a responsibility to support the existence research and for primary process and, as well, for meaningful unconscious mentation, theorists and researchers have expanded their focus to include “empirical investigations, evolutionary considerations, the operation of conditioning, and vexing issues in the philosophy of mind and the philosophy of action” (p. 183).

For Michael Robbins, Freud’s discovery of the unconscious as a source of energy and content includes the components for “two embryonic mind-models that he was unable to separate sufficiently that each might be elaborated and built upon” (p. 196). Robbins has elaborated the less recognized of these models, primordial consciousness, as “a form of consciousness different from reflective symbolic thought; a mental activity that is ubiquitous in human affairs both normal and pathological” (p. 196). He describes subsequent attempts to separate from Freud by proposing variations on this primordial consciousness, but have succeeded only in reformulating the original concept.

Wilma Bucci concludes her article with a critique of the conventional theory of primary process. The view that primary process reflects only disorganization and a need to be bound or discharged lest it impinge on productive thought reflects fundamental inconsistencies within psychoanalytic theory. She notes that even within classical discussions of dream work, primary process carries the characteristics of regulation by consistent laws, mechanisms of its own, and not meaninglessness, but a particular kind of meaning. She concludes that rather than disorder, primary process provides, viewed through a lens of affective activation, a distinct and valuable dimension of mental activity. That dimension, viewed through a lens of affective activation, “occurs in adaptive, mature, rational, waking life; is associated with highly advanced forms of reasoning and problem solving; and may develop in complexity as the individual matures” (p. 208).

Epilogue: Safety—The Patient, The Analyst, The Dyad

Carol Levin and Estelle Shane

Estelle Shane

Estelle Shane  

We decided to conclude this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry: Safety—The Patient, The Analyst, The Dyad, in which our topic has been reviewed historically and explored so movingly, and perhaps definitively for this moment in time, by our contributors, Joseph Lichtenberg, Elizabeth Carr and Janna Sandmeyer, Roger Segalla, Jr., Hazel Ipp, Amy Eldridge, and Joye Weisel-Barth, with a case discussion1 that vividly captures what Segalla has called the “safety-danger dialectic dynamic” (this issue, p. 576) and places us live in the midst of it in all its complexity.

Estelle treated Oliver a long time ago. He was a man who had been traumatized as a child and who experienced helpless rage at his therapist because he was convinced that she neither knew nor understood him. Her case discussion illuminates so many of the themes explored by the articles in this issue, for example the disorganizing effect that traumatic affect and fear has on each of member of the dyad and on their relationship, the stall in development when fear and rage saturate the climate in the room, the responsibility of the patient for the safety of the dyad and furthering the work. By “voting with [his] feet,” as Carr and Sandmeyer felicitously call it (this issue, p. 560)—Oliver kept coming—he contributed all that he could for the furtherance of the analytic work if it was to be authentic.

Estelle and Oliver found their way out of their impasse by their commitment to each other, their endurance, tolerance, in effect their good will. And Estelle’s relentless honesty. She faced Oliver’s escalating onslaughts head on, without shrinking from them in spite of her own fear. And Estelle was ultimately able to find the words to help her patient mentalize and integrate the experience that had emerged in the consulting room and, by thus doing, helped Oliver to contain it, following implicitly Slade’s recommendation (2014). Estelle and Oliver both grew from their immersion in their cocreated cauldron of fire and their emergence from it.

On the Unique Power of Free-Associative Discourse: Notes on the Contributions of Henry Zvi Lothane and Christopher Bollas

Barnaby B. Barratt PHD DHS

Barnaby B. Barratt

The Heritage Stone House, 122 Virginia Avenue, Parkmore (JHB), 2196, South Africa
BBBarratt@earthlink.net

Barnaby B. Barratt   Director of Studies, Parkmore Institute; Training Analyst, South African Psychoanalytic Association; and Senior Research Fellow, Wits Institute for Social and Economic Research, University of Witwatersrand

It is argued that the method of free association is, as Freud suggested, the sine qua non of psychoanalysis. Appreciation is expressed for the different ways in which writers such as Lothane and Bollas have argued this position. Lothane’s article is then used as a platform from which to elaborate the thesis that there is no psychoanalysis without the praxis of free-association and its attendant auxiliary notions of resistance and repression. The argument draws on Barratt’s previous writings on this topic concerning the way in which only the free-associative method comprises a de-repressive method of discursive speaking, listening, and opening to desire that is otherwise than representationality.

Prologue: Daniel Stern: Contributions to Psychoanalysis and Developmental Psychology, Part II

Patricia Nachman PHD and Elizabeth Carr A.P.R.N., M.S.N., B.C.

Elizabeth Carr

Elizabeth Carr  

This issue is the second of two issues to pay tribute to the work of Daniel Stern. The personal tributes of Robert Emde and Nadia Bruschweiler-Stern launched the first issue, which gave a rare view into the person, and the work of Dan Stern. The articles in Part I highlighted Stern’s early work using the micro-analytic method he developed to explore the interactions between babies and mothers. This work provided a fine-grained view of how the baby can maintain and moderate the flow of social exchange and how the mother contributes to the reciprocal communication process with each partner changing with the other.

In addition, articles by Beatrice Beebe, Dan Schechter, and Elisabeth Fivaz provided empirical examples and new clinical understandings about interpersonal relationships and clinical interventions that evolved from use of the micro-analytic method. To further his ideas, Stern posed new questions about the development of a sense of self that went beyond traditionally accepted viewpoints. Bob Michels’ article commented on these ideas.

This issue, Part II, addresses Stern’s later work and the work he did in collaboration with the Boston Change Process Study Group (BCPSG). This issue is introduced by a tribute to Stern by his colleagues in the Boston group.

Together, the work of the BCPSG presents a conceptual framework for the question of what creates change in psychoanalysis and concludes that something more than interpretation is needed to bring about change. They propose that the something more resides in the interactional intersubjective processes that give rise to what they call “implicit relational knowing” (BCPSG, 2010, p. 5) or, the implicit, procedural processes occurring between partners in a relationship. In the analytic relationship, it comprises moments between the patient and therapist when something new is created in the relationship that alters the intersubjective environment. This is a reciprocal process in which change takes place in the implicit relationship at “moments of meeting” through alternations in “ways of being with” (BCPSG, 2010, pp. 6–7).

Epilogue: Daniel Stern: Contributions to Psychoanalysis and Developmental Psychology, Part II

Elizabeth Carr A.P.R.N., M.S.N., B.C. and Patricia Nachman PHD

Patricia Nachman

Patricia Nachman   Patricia Nachman, Ph.D. patnachman@gmail.com 51 East 78th Street, # 4-C, New York, NY 10075.

The second issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry honoring Daniel Stern reflects on a number of important contributions Stern made to developmental psychology and to psychoanalysis. We begin this issue with a remembrance from the Boston Change Process Study Group describing Stern’s playful, generous manner and his pioneering work synthesizing developmental research and psychoanalytic thinking. This article provides a wonderful sense of what it was like to be with and to work with Dan, highlighting his creativity and sense of fun.

What follows are three articles that explore and expand Stern’s concept of implicit relational knowing. Ted Shapiro, writing from a classical psychoanalytic model, provides a respectful critique that, nonetheless, includes his appreciation of the relevance of now moments that may contribute to a new opening in the intersubjective space between patient and analyst, potentially leading to a deeper engagement between patient and analyst. A second article, from Bruce Reis, incorporates a philosophical perspective, calling for a deep connectedness between patient and analyst. Reis promotes the importance of the analyst deeply being with her patient. Massimo Ammaniti concludes this section with an article that provides a broad developmental exploration of implicit knowledge. Ammaniti includes a clinical vignette that illustrates the emergence of new ways of being and being together for Ammaniti and his patient.

In the next section, three articles explore Stern’s construct of dynamic forms of vitality from a number of perspectives. Myron Hofer explores the concept of vitality forms from an evolutionary perspective including their role in the development of complex adult social interactions in primates. Vittorio Gallese and Magali Rochat discuss the topic of forms of vitality from a neuroscience perspective and offer a new take on the elements of making others’ behavior meaningful, the process of social cognition. They also include a discussion of social cognition deficits in individuals affected by the autism spectrum disorder. In the final article of this section, Arnold Modell provides his perspective on musical speech as essential for recognizing the inner state and intentions of another.

Prologue: Primary Process Revisited

Lester Lenoff LCSWIssue Editor

Lester Lenoff

Lester Lenoff   CONTACT Lester Lenoff, LCSW lstrlenoff@gmail.com 150 East 57th Street, Apt. 24AB, New York, NY 10022.

In agreeing to edit this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry, I sought to locate contributors who would reconsider one of Freud’s foundational innovations, the concept of primary process. Analytic lore, the common or shared knowledge in the field, privileges secondary process, consensually validated “reality,” over primary process, instinctually driven impulses or, following the relational turn, compulsively re-enacted, distorted relational schema. And in this issue, each author, in her or his own way, accomplishes that.

Linda Brakel comes closest to Freud’s initial formulation. Primary and secondary process remain distinct in their mode of operation. Primary process tolerates opposites, contradictions coexist, and reality testing and time contextualizing are suspended. “Primary-process mentation is faster, closer to the drives, affect and impulse-linked” (p. 177). Primary process underlies the clinically key concept of transference, in that “categorizations, too, are associatively constructed” on the basis of “small, superficial, or insignificant features” (p. 177). Within this context, Brakel seeks to provide an interdisciplinary basis for the use of primary process as “a gateway to general understanding of mentation in humans, and in many nonhuman species, as well” (p. 178).

Arising from extensive experience with all aspects of treating schizophrenic patients, Michael Robbins argues that as a result of Freud’s identifying consciousness with reflective symbolic thought, the role of primary process has remained obscure. He proposes that rather than differing in quality from consciousness, primary process represents a developmentally prior, or primordial, form of symbolic thought. He explores the frameworks offered by Freud, Klein, Bion, and Matte-Blanco, arriving at “a model that clarifies that [primary process] is conscious and has cognitive-affective-sensory-perceptual-motor principles of operation that make its presence knowable across a wide spectrum of human phenomena both normal and pathological” (p. 193).

The Primary Process: Bridges to Interdisciplinary Studies of Mind

Linda Brakel MD

Linda Brakel

Linda Brakel   Linda A. W. Brakel, M.D., is the author of many interdisciplinary articles and three books—Philosophy, Psychoanalysis, and the A-Rational Mind (Oxford, 2009); Unconscious Knowing and Other Essays in Psycho-Philosophical Analysis (Oxford, 2010); and The Ontology of Psychology (Routledge, 2013). She has also co-authored three other volumes. Brakel is an Associate Professor (adj) of Psychiatry, and a Faculty Research Associate in Philosophy at the University of Michigan. She is also a faculty member of the Michigan Psychoanalytic Institute.CONTACT Linda A. W. Brakel, M.D. brakel@umich.edu 525 Third Street, Ann Arbor, MI 48103.

Psychoanalytic theory is one of the world’s grand theories. Not merely clinical, psychoanalytic general theory introduces two momentous contributions. One, the key role of primary processes, is the subject of this issue and this article. Here I maintain that primary processes are a-rational, not irrational, hence not pathological, but developmental, and prevalent also in nonhuman animals. I review empirical evidence supporting the existence of such primary process mentation. Brief accounts are then given of several interdisciplinary bridges to mind and behavior studies based on this expanded view of a-rational primary processes. Interdisciplinary areas discussed range from the biological (conditioning and evolutionary considerations) to vexing issues in the philosophy of mind and the philosophy of action (agency and belief).

Working with couples from a classical perspective can be thought of as an oxymoron, unlike working from object relations and relational viewpoints, often seen to be the more natural fits. This article offers a fresh look at those parts of the classical perspective that relate very clearly to working with two partners in a couple. Freud’s theories in Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality (1905) and On Narcissism (1914a) provide theoretical background for the work. Concepts such as transference (between partners, between the partner[s] and the therapist) and countertransference are shown to be manifested in complex ways with couples. Being mindful of unresolved developmental issues—for example, Oedipal and separation-individuation issues—which may have played a part in partner choice and in the resulting problems, allows the therapist to offer deep interpretations of within- and between-partner conflicts. Interestingly, unresolved Oedipal issues, particularly, may form an important part of the countertransference.

Melvin Bornstein MD

Melvin Bornstein

625 Purdy Street, Birmingham, MI 48009
melvinbornstein@gmail.com

Melvin Bornstein  

When Henry Lothane approached me with the suggestion of creating an issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry devoted to free associations, I thought it would be an interesting project of focusing on an original clinical idea and following it to the present. I could not have imagined that this Freudian concept had such power to bridge the objective and subjective, but, more importantly, to touch the heart and soul of being human.

As I first read the articles in this issue, my thoughts took me to Jonathan Lear’s (1990) first book, Love and Its Place in Nature, where he argued that Freud began a revolution, the results of which have been barely realized. Freud showed us that by using psychoanalysis as a method, we have within our grasp a science of subjectivity.

My thoughts then took me to Seven Brief Lessons on Physics written by Carlos Rovelli (2014), a theoretical physicist, head of the Gravity Group at the Centre de Physique Theorique of Aix-Marseille University, one of the founders of the loop quantum gravity theory.

With the help of a progression of theories—Newtonian, Relativity, and Quantum Mechanics—he wrote:

Nature is our home, and in nature we are at home. This strange and multicolored, and astonishing world that we explore—where space is granular, time does not exist, and things are nowhere—is not something that estranges us from or true selves, for this is only what our natural curiosity revels to us about the place of our dwelling. About the stuff which we ourselves are made. We are made of the same stardust of which all things are made and when we are immersed in suffering or when we are experiencing intense joy, we are being nothing other than what we can’t help but be part of our world. [Rovelli, 2014, p. 79]

Then my thoughts led me to Gerald Edelman (1992), who formulated that the mind arises from the billions of neural loops transmitting impulses in such rapidity and intensity that mind is created which is something like a holograph.

Then the idea came to me that the neurophysiological models which begin in our minds must have the imprint of the model of the mind that we are using at the time.

Prologue: Reflections on Jane Lewis’s “Bodies in Dialogue: Empathic Connectedness in the Realm of the Unspeakable”

Melvin Bornstein MD

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein   CONTACT Melvin Bornstein, M.D. melvinbornstein@gmail.com 625 Purdy Street, Birmingham, MI 48009.

Understanding the relationship between the mind and the body has been a mystery for scientists, philosophers, and theologians since humans first began questioning the meaning of life. It was this mystery that drove Freud to discover psychoanalysis and theorize that the drives were forces that bridged the body and mind. In this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry, we guide the reader into the very same mystery, only with a century and a half of psychoanalytic experience.

We begin with Jane Lewis’s article, “Bodies in Dialogue: Empathic Connectedness in the Realm of the Unspeakable,” which is about a treatment of a traumatized man with long periods of silence. Because of the mutuality within the treatment relationship, Lewis can demonstrate the silence as nonverbal communication in the response to trauma. The trauma infuses the body and mind, which become part of the therapeutic relationship that includes the transference. Communication about the patient’s present, past, and transference becomes the source of transformation that leads to change by bridging the mind and body in both patient and Lewis.

The contributors to this issue had the challenge to turn to the richness of contemporary psychoanalytic thinking to discuss the clinical material of the mind-body connection and unconscious communication. Of great importance have been the insights from infant-mother interaction, where body and mind play such an important role; the advances in understanding early mental life such as the development of mentalization, the structure of the Self from Self Psychology and a Self as an agency that brings us closer to conceptualizing the person as central in interaction and engagement has altered the landscape of mental life.

The usefulness of conceptual tools that are now available to communicate and understand unconscious communication has been challenging. This is especially true within the realm of intersubjectivity, where self and other, different affects, past and present, objectivity and subjectivity have porous boundaries. We are just beginning to understand the place of the body that is not only separated from the mind, but part of the mind, which demands a change from a process that is linear to one of three and four dimensions with ties to culture and one’s legacy. This is only some of the important areas of advances to help us understand Jane Lewis’s therapeutic process.

The description of a psychoanalysis has changed dramatically during the last 150 years. As these articles reveal, it is especially apparent when the psychoanalysis must address trauma that is connected to bodily reactions. It is here that we can glimpse of the complexity of the patients’ and analysts’ intimate experiences with each other. Nothing is more apparent than in trying to explain the complexity of the mind and body from moment to moment in analytic work.

We see that the description must be intersubjective to grasp the intimacy and the deep effect of the experience on the patient and the analyst in which mutuality is integral, especially, because the analytic process by its very nature is a developmental that leads to transformations.

In the therapeutic process that unfolds between her patient and Jane Lewis we find references to a therapist’s attitude that points to a relational stance; in particular, the therapist finds inside herself the way to unblock the patient’s ‘frozen’ situation. Thanks to the therapist’s subjectivity, the intersubjective field is animated with images that can reveal something about the patient’s experience of terror and abandonment. This article offers a comparison between two different strategies for clinical attention. The author compares his lens shaped by a musical metaphor of “polyrhythmic patterning” on embodied registrations which he describes as “fluidity” in contrast to a lens of structures or categories of experience. He then contrasts this lens to that offered by Lewis which she describes with the metaphor of an “imaginary camera” with which she creates “snapshots” as representations of unbearable (and often unformulated) trauma shaped by the patient's narrative and her own trauma history. Acknowledging the exquisite connection between analyst and patient, the author uses 2 clinical moments to further illustrate the benefits of each metaphoric lens for possible analytic work.

Enhancing the Dyad: The Benefits of Combining Group Therapy with Psychoanalytic Treatment

Andrew Smolar MD

Andrew Smolar

Andrew Smolar   Andrew I. Smolar, M.D., is Training and Supervising Analyst and Current President, Psychoanalytic Center of Philadelphia; and Associate Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Temple University.CONTACT Andrew I. Smolar, M.D. ahzsmolar@verizon.net The Wynnewood House, 300 East Lancaster Avenue, #209, Wynnewood, PA 19096.

In this article, I consider the benefits of adding group therapy to psychoanalytic treatment. I describe the evolution of combined treatment, advantages of the group modality, and some of the reasons for therapists’ resistance to it. Through clinical example, I describe developmental blocks that became clear during a patient’s analysis, countertransference responses I became aware of during the analysis, and my assessment of the potential risks and benefits of adding group therapy. I then describe how some of the patient’s developmental blocks were engaged after the addition of group therapy, particularly highlighting the to-and-fro between modalities during working-through. Subsequent discussion addresses the indications for the addition of group therapy, specific therapeutic elements gained through combined treatment, and technical challenges confronting the combined therapist.

The Primary Process: Freud’s Profound Yet Neglected Contribution to the Psychology of Consciousness

Michael Robbins

Michael Robbins

Michael Robbins   Michael Robbins was formerly Professor of Clinical Psychiatry at Harvard Medical School, McLean Hospital, and UCSF at Langley-Porter Hospital. He is a member of the Boston Psychoanalytic Society and International Psychoanalytic Association. He is author of four books, most recently (2018) Consciousness, Language, and Self, and numerous articles, book chapters and reviews. He currently lives and practices in Amherst, Massachusetts.CONTACT Michael Robbins mdrobbinsmd@comcast.net 56 Kestrel Lane, Amherst, MA 01002.

The primary process model is part of Freud’s struggle to define and distinguish conscious and unconscious mental activity. He created two embryonic models of unconscious mind. One he derived from studying symptoms of dynamic repression or sequestration of content already capable of symbolic mental representation. The other, the primary process, is his landmark effort to define a mental activity different from reflective representational thought, derived from studying dreaming. He could not clearly separate the repression model, as it is also based on the primary process. He vacillated as to whether the primary process is qualitatively different from representational symbolic thought. His efforts to articulate preconscious mentation suggest an ambiguous gray area between conscious thought and the primary process. Although he concluded that the primary process is unconscious because it is not intrinsically reflective, its manifestations are psychologically conscious and directly evident except in the physiologically unconscious state of dreaming. Similar problems color the efforts of others including Klein, Matte-Blanco, and theorists of attachment and implicit learning to separate conscious and unconscious mind and to articulate a model of mental function different from reflective consciousness. A model of conscious mental activity different from reflective representational consciousness, called primordial consciousness, is proposed to account for a wide spectrum of human phenomena both normal and pathological that share characteristics of immediacy and belief. They include, in addition to dreaming, psychosis, creativity, spirituality, and mental process in non-western cultures.

Daniel N. Stern, M.D., A Remembrance

Jeremy Nahum M.D., for the Boston Change Process Study Group

Jeremy Nahum

Jeremy Nahum   CONTACT Jeremy Nahum, M.D. jpnahum@massmed.org 83 Cambridge Parkway, Cambridge, MA 02142.

For the last 18 years of Dan’s life, he was a consummate intellectual force in the Boston Change Process Study Group as we grappled with how developmental research could be used to understand change processes in psychodynamic and other forms of therapy. In his pioneering work synthesizing developmental and psychoanalytic thinking, he blazed a path for us all, and his thinking profoundly affected generations of psychoanalysts and developmental psychologists. Since the early 1970s, Dan made creative and seminal contributions at the interface of psychoanalysis and developmental psychology. By the 1990s, this work was so seminal that it called for basic changes in the older theoretical framework of psychoanalysis. The Change Process Group formed around this need and gathered together a diverse group of psychoanalytic and developmental thinkers with often divergent views about how to pursue such a goal. This endeavor seemed, to some observers, to be a grandiose and impossible task at best, and at worst, possibly a breeding ground for intense intellectual conflict and frustration. It proved to be the adventure of a lifetime.

Dan was intellectually fearless, willing and able to play with ideas openly with us. It was his signature, the signature of a creative person. He was unfazed, unthreatened when his ideas were disputed or scorned, and welcomed reasoned rebuttals. You could say to him, “Dan that doesn’t make any sense for x y z reasons,” and he’d say, “OK, how about a or b instead”—with a mischievous glint in his eye. Not surprisingly, within the group there were frequent spirited intellectual disagreements. Dan would disarm those in contention and charm us away from those conflictual moments, diffusing the rancor. It meant that disagreement remained intellectual, rather than becoming personal, an important condition for the intense engagement of strong-minded thinkers. Attacks from outside critics whom he considered uninformed were countered with a steely determination and a refusal to back down, even in the face of powerful opponents. Dan was a consummate performer. As the keynote speaker at a meeting of the American Psychoanalytic Association in Seattle in 2005, he made a point about irreversibility; from the lecturn, he poured a glass of water on the floor in a slow consistent stream startling the audience. He got the audience’s attention and made his point in memorable fashion. Dan somehow enabled those around him to feel enhanced, inspired by him.

Death as the Ultimate Castration

Martin Silverman MD

Martin Silverman

Martin Silverman   Martin A. Silverman, M.D., is a training and supervising analyst and supervising child analyst at the Institute for Psychoanalytic Education affiliated with the NYU School of Medicine and a training and supervising analyst at the Center for Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy of New Jersey. He is the Associate Editor and Book Review Editor of The Psychoanalytic Quarterly.CONTACT Martin A. Silverman, M.D. Martinsilverman31@gmail.com 551 Ridgewood Road, Maplewood, NJ 07040.

Psychoanalysts, beginning with Sigmund Freud, have been scanting, denying, minimizing, and obfuscating the significance of fear of death in their patients and in themselves. Starting with Freud, they have tended to interpret fear of death as a displacement from other sources of anxiety, especially from castration anxiety. Conversely, some psychoanalysts and psychotherapists have denied the presence or significance of castration anxiety in their patients and in themselves. In this communication, the prevalence and significance of each of these forms of terror are examined, individually and as to their connection with one another. Considerable clinical, child observational, and literary evidence is presented that illustrates the significance and meaning of these two sources of terror within the human psyche, as well as the relationship which they have with one another.

Prologue: Sex, Gender, and Identity

S. Katz Ph.D., LPIssue Editor

S. Katz

S. Katz   CONTACT S. Montana Katz, Ph.D., LP smkatz2@verizon.net 611 Broadway, Suite 520, New York, NY 10012.

In this issue, contributors were asked to consider the concept of castration anxiety in light of contemporary psychoanalytic thought and practice. Freud’s original formulations of castration anxiety assumed a model of sex and gender identification that does not correspond with contemporary experience or understanding of the complexities involved. The range of possible sex and gender identifications as complex combinations of sex plus gender self-identifications is noted in many of the contributions.

In Rosemary Balsam’s contribution, reference is made to the shift from a “one sex” to a “two sex” model. In both Balsam and Marie Rudden’s articles there is discussion of female genital anxiety, rather than castration anxiety. Cultural factors play a prominent role in Anna Migliozzi’s article. Danielle Knafo emphasizes relational experience in castration anxiety and focuses on transsexual experience in a case study. Martin Silverman explores the relationship of castration and death anxieties. Nicola Abel-Hirsch relates a Bionian perspective and Patricia Gherovici explores the perspective of the later work of Lacan. Jani Santamaría offers two clinical cases that demonstrate the life-long nature of struggles with castration anxiety.

In this prologue, a structure is suggested for understanding the range of complexities involved in sex, sexuality, and gender identity formation and the contributions to this issue are described. An aspect of early, pre-Oedipal development is described, which has been called the Electral phase. In formulating this early developmental process and its consolidation into a dynamic constellation called the Electra complex, paths of initial sex and gender identity emerge. The Electral phase is proposed as resulting in sex and gender self-identification and contains antecedents to the Oedipal phase, a subsequent, and often overlapping, part of the process of identity formation. To describe the Electral phase, this discussion will focus on early phases of life, both in utero and after birth existence.

As the contributions to this issue demonstrate, with the evolving understanding of sex and gender identification, together with modifications in clinical models in contemporary psychoanalysis, the clinical concept of castration anxiety remains relevant and useful. Cases presented in this issue showed how employing the concept of castration anxiety was central to understanding the patients’ struggles.

The contributions also indicate future directions for continuing to evolve the psychoanalytic understanding of the interplay of sex, sexuality, and gender with castration, separation, and death anxiety.

Henry Zvi Lothane  

In this issue, we are pleased to present a number of operational descriptions of the method of free association, an inescapable topic in any discussion of therapy and theory. We also offer a rainbow of opinions for and against, reflecting the concord and conflict all along the history of psychoanalysis as a method and a movement, i.e., establishment. But in this context, a major difference leaps to mind: Disagreement about theory, e.g., the sexual theory of neurosis, has been the cause of ideological splits and cruel and costly internecine wars between orthodox Freudians and neo-Freudian heretics, as between Freud and Adler and Freud and Jung over the libido theory (Lothane, 1997a). Such rivalry was also seen in the past polarization between the American Psychoanalytic Association and the American Academy of Psychoanalysis or between the Deutsche Psychoanalytische Gesellschaft (DPG) and the Deutsche Psychoanalytische Vereinigung (DPV). The disagreements about free association have been rather civil, compared to those over theory.

To associate means to place together, to connect, in action or in thought. The activity of associating takes place all the time in every sphere of psychological life: in sense-perception (both as cognition and re-cognition), imagination, memory, habit formation, problem solving, scientific (Helmholtz, Poincaré) and literary creativity, and, last but not least, in every conversation—it is that basic. Intellectualist approaches to associating usually leave out feelings and emotions; however, verbal and nonverbal communication of emotions is an integral part of the flow of associations.

Associative thinking has been discussed by philosophers since Aristotle; by psychologists, e.g., William James’ “stream of thought” (1890, Chapter IX) and Charles Peirce in 1902: “If after any thought, the current of ideas flows freely, it follows the law of mental association” (cited in Buchler, 1955, p. 233); and illustrated by writers, e.g., James Joyce’s Ulysses (1922). In the psychoanalytic setting, called free association, it is basic to the process of interchanges between the analysand and analyst in a special state of mind called free-floating attention.

Reflections on Safety

Joseph Lichtenberg MD

Joseph Lichtenberg

Joseph Lichtenberg   Joseph D. Lichtenberg, M.D., is the editor-in-chief of Psychoanalytic Inquiry.CONTACT Joseph D. Lichtenberg, M.D. joelichtenberg@aol.com 6256 Clearwood Road, Bethesda, MD 20817.

Psychoanalysis began as a science-based attempt to understand and explain the anxieties and conflicts that drove many patients to hysterical and other symptomatic expressions. Consequently, safety, although implied as the obverse of anxiety, played little or no direct role in Freud’s formulations. Originally, when affects were regarded as derivatives of drives, safety didn’t have a place in the theory. Freud’s emphasis was on sexual excitement, anxiety and guilt, love and hate, mourning and melancholia. Later theorists moved shame, embarrassment and humiliation, and pride and idealization to the fore.

Safety entered the more traditional psychoanalytic theory with a paper by Joseph Sandler on the background of safety, in 1960. Sandler placed safety as the affect that determined whether preconscious contents would be allowed to enter conscious awareness. The strongest argument for safety as a key affect or mental state derives from attachment research and theory. Bowlby and his followers regarded the goal of infants’ seeking behavior and the mother’s response to be the safety gained from the establishment of a secure base at times of danger and loss. A contemporary view of the basis for children seeking intimate relationships would draw on many sources: attachment theory’s seeking a secure base and a sense of safety; self psychology’s seeking of experiences of mirroring, twinship sharing, and idealization; and the traditional emphasis on the desire for sensual enjoyment and physiological requirements. Jay Greenberg (1991) proposed safety and effectance as dual drives. Emmanuel Ghent (2002) proposed homeostatic safety and expansion of functions as two types of needs. I and my colleagues (Lichtenberg et al., 1996; Lichtenberg, 2005) have suggested that, for both analyst and analysand, a sense of safety is an essential feature of the frame that makes analysis possible, and that, in an ongoing analysis, a background of safety provides the basis for an analysand to risk the revelations necessary for progress.

Henry Zvi Lothane MD

Henry Zvi Lothane

1435 Lexington Avenue, New York, NY 10128

Henry Zvi Lothane   Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York

Freud established psychoanalysis as a historical science and free association as its basic method of healing and research, differentiating a theory of method from theories of disorder. Psychoanalytic therapy was based on the fundamental rule of free association as an indispensable instrument for decoding and interpreting such phenomena as dreams, daydreams, hallucinations, delusions, and enactments occurring in various normal and pathological states, juxtaposing formulaic interpretations with free associations and process interventions. It was embraced by the first (Ferenczi, Jung) and second generation (Reik, Isakower) followers of Freud, and by contemporary analysts. The evolution of free association in Freud is surveyed during four periods and themes: (a) the prepsychoanalytic, 1888–1892; (b) 1893–1895, in the Studies on Hysteria; (c) 1900 in The Interpretation of Dreams; and (d) 1912–1915 in the papers on technique. The purpose of this article is to validate free association as a method for exploration of unconscious processes, to ground the psychoanalytic method as historical, and address the question is Freud’s working out of free association still relevant today.

Castration anxiety is a contentious issue for contemporary psychoanalysis and necessarily occupies a central position in the theory that Freud developed, at the crossroad between the individual and his desires, the individual and his sexuality, and the individual and civilization. In this wider sense, castration anxiety describes a state of mind in which individuals, women as well as men, must battle throughout the course of their lives against limitations and, hence, so-called safe pleasures (security, reproduction, family, etc.) brought about through the constraints imposed on them by civilization. From this perspective, castration anxiety can be seen as a primary gesture toward a sexuality that becomes enmeshed in conflict and obscured by a sense of shame and guilt. Exploring the works of contemporary British artist Sarah Lucas, the Italian writer A. Moravia, and the Italian director M. Ferreri, followed by a series of brief clinical vignettes, I underline and discuss the oppositional and unfulfillable search for lust encapsulated in Freud’s castration anxiety concept and the eternal mysteriousness of sexuality.

Wilma Bucci PHD

Wilma Bucci

Wilma Bucci   Wilma Bucci, Ph.D., is Professor Emerita, Derner Institute, Adelphi University; Director of Research, Pacella Research Center, New York Psychoanalytic Society and Institute; Honorary Member of APsaA, NYPSI, and IPTAR; and author of Psychoanalysis and Cognitive Science and many other publications.CONTACT Wilma Bucci, Ph.D. wbucci@icloud.com Pacella Research Center, New York Psychoanalytic Society and Institute, 247 E. 82nd Street, New York, NY 10028.

The initial defining framework of the primary process based on flow of psychic energy has been largely rejected by contemporary psychoanalytic theorists, but the concept remains in use clinically, particularly in application to the flow of associations and the interpretation of dreams. Some researchers have attempted to characterize primary process thought in terms of contents and formal properties of thought without reference to the energy framework, but this approach fails to account for the role of emotional intensity in mental life. The integration of affective arousal with particular properties of thought that is central to the primary process concept can be understood today in the context of current research in cognitive psychology, emotion theory, and neuroscience. The version of multiple code theory outlined here provides a framework for the involvement of affect in productive and complex mental operations in areas from sports and the arts to scientific discovery, as well as therapy, and also provides a basis for empirical research.

Daniel Goldin MFT, Psy.D.

Daniel Goldin

During dreaming, the brain inhibits input from the senses and blocks motor output. The miracle is that, despite a lack of contact with the senses and a temporary paralysis, the brain continues to generate densely meaningful first-person scenarios. What justifies this purely imaginative procedure that leaves people so vulnerable to predators? A great deal of neuroanatomical evidence suggests that during REM sleep, the brain prunes exuberant synaptic connections. In so doing, the brain simplifies overly complex models of the world formed during the day to deal with noisy scenarios and renders them more generalizable to the future. Freud likened the mandate of dreaming to the task an illustrator faces in coming up with a single illustration to represent the day’s headlines. In my view, this process of condensation is not a method of disguise, as Freud believed, but the very function of dreaming, and it has a temporal signature. Dreams reveal and simplify past happenings by generating tight fictional narratives around similar schemas, exposing by analogy the deep invariant structures of the stories by which people organize their lives.

The Phoenix myth is commonly thought of as a simple Egyptian parable of re-incarnation. In contrast, this analytic dyad found that the visual images evoked by its elaborated mythemes (sub-plots) related to the various existential moods and affects characteristic of trauma identified by Stolorow (2007), suggesting a psychological purpose, that of emotional self-renewal. Mythology has most consistently been adopted for use in Jung’s analytical psychology, but this article demonstrates this myth’s usefulness with a contemporary relational psychoanalytic approach, that of intersubjective-systems theory. This was effective for an analysand whose former analysis had been abruptly terminated. It was found that the dialogic exploration of possible meaning in the mythemes brought dissociated experience into language, assisted with the emotional integration of the trauma, and restored the analysand’s diminished sense-of-being. Images bring together diverse somatic, cognitive, and verbal information, normally separated into different communication “codes” (Bucci, 1997a). This ancient myth’s longevity may be due to a useful psychological function; its images can aid the organizing of unformulated unconscious chaotic experience and assist in the process of bringing dissociated or preverbal emotions and moods into language. The utility of the Phoenix myth in a relational dialogical process that helps symbolize unsymbolized unconscious content could assist in work with other survivors of catastrophic loss.

Following the idea of Green about whether sexuality is related to psychoanalysis, I begin this article with a question that refers to the title of the work: “Has castration anxiety anything to do with psychoanalysis?” Concerned about the lack of bibliographic reference to the concept of castration anxiety, I make a tour of the notion, taking as its point of departure and arrival the intellectual itinerary of Freud. I continue with a brief review of later authors. Interested in rethinking this issue, I wonder whether castration anxiety is expressed in the same manner in the clinical practice of today. The question does not tolerate a hasty response, so I present two clinical vignettes to call attention to castration anxiety as a central factor in the development and understanding of the clinical practice. The last section refers to the discussion and concluding reflections.

In describing her work with her traumatized patient Antonio, Dr. Jane Lewis focuses on Barthes’s (1981) notion of a photograph as having the symbolic linking function of an umbilical cord, and emphasizes the notion of the punctum, the specific personal wounding detail in an image that connects to the viewer’s experience. This article discusses these ideas, which appear mystical to Lewis, in the contexts of the theory of multiple coding and the referential process, as well as recent advances in the fields of social neuroscience and embodied communication. In the early Arousal phase of the referential process, emotion schemas associated with painful events of the past are activated for both participants, in subsymbolic, embodied form. Antonio is largely mute and frozen; Lewis also feels herself freezing and disappearing. In the Symbolizing phase, Antonio begins to connect to dreaded experience of his past, and to tell memories, fantasies and dreams. Memories and images of her past, related emotionally to Antonio’s experience, are awakened for Lewis as well. Through their embodied communication and shared imagery, the therapist’s ability to find emotional meaning for her own painful experience appears to support the patient’s beginning to provide some meaning for his pain and dread. Related observations by Bollas and Arlow, and parallels to a case reported by Ogden are discussed.

This article reviews Freud’s theory of castration, as well as critiques of the theory. I then offer my own elaboration of castration theory, proposing that castration fantasies are universal and refer to a sense of incompleteness—about the body as well as psychic attributes—in both males and females. Such fantasies, I argue, deal with the gap between what one is and what one would like to be and are frequently expressed in envy toward perceived privileges belonging to persons of the opposite sex, same sex, and different generation. Furthermore, these fantasies are intimately tied to object relations. A case of a transgender male who desired castration is presented to illustrate this expanded theory and its usefulness.

In his introduction to The Interpersonal World of the Infant (1985), Dan Stern stated, “As an infant I spent considerable time in the hospital, and in order to know what was going on, I became a watcher, a reader of the non verbal” (p. ix). He viewed the implicit nonverbal as a necessary complement to the explicit verbal dialogue, the subject matter of psychoanalysis. The communication of vitality affects could be thought of as the relational element in speech. As I understand his concept of vitality affects, he was not referring to a specific emotion, but to a transcendent communicative function of a range of affects that convey the vital state of the other.

Regarding this concept of vitality affects, Modell acknowledged that he was influenced by the contribution of the philosopher Suzanne Langer, who suggested that works of art convey the feeling of “felt life.” Unlike a specific emotion such as anxiety or anger, vitality affects are more global, conveying an overall state of being in relation to the other (Stern, 1985). In this, I believe that he was influenced by Andre Green’s concept of the “dead mother” (Green, 1986).

I suggest that the vitality of the other is communicated by the musical qualities of speech. This is in accord with the work of the infant researcher Colwyn Trevarthen. In this tribute to the work of Dan Stern, I focus on the function of music as a primordial means of conveying meaning. I believe, along with the anthro-paleontologist Steven Mithen (2006), that musical communication in modern speech is a vestige of human phylogenetic inheritance. There is a strong inference that musical communication existed in earlier species of mankind prior to the development of language (embracing words and grammar). With the advent of homo sapiens, the earlier musical form of communication rode piggy back, as it were, upon spoken language, as it does today. There is considerable evidence that infants infer meaning from the musical qualities of infant directed speech. This occurs within a few weeks after birth (Gratier and Trevarthen, 2008). As there is not sufficient time for learning, it must represent an inherent capacity. Through musical speech, the vital inner state of the other is communicated. I suggest that this intersubjective system of communication is an expression of Dan Stern’s vitality affects.

This systematic review of contributions to peer-reviewed journals in the area of couple interventions aims to provide a comprehensive and intensive overview of this evolving field, within psychoanalysis. Using a pan theoretical systematic review methodology, 113 peer-reviewed journal articles were reviewed, dated between 1963 and 2014, addressing the topic of couple therapy and psychoanalysis. This article addresses a number of specific questions including, where authors have published their work, what methodologies they have used, with which couples psychoanalysts have been working, how writers from within different theoretical orientations talk about their work with couples, and how the field has changed over time. It also explores emerging themes of the relationship between couple and individual therapy, sex, and co-therapy. This review of writing over the past 50 years suggests that although Classical contributions have waned over time, couple psychoanalysts from within Object Relations, Self Psychology, Intersubjectivity, and Relational orientations have evolved in their discourse about couple distress, from an application of psychoanalytic concepts to full-bodied, well-articulated, clear, and concise approaches to diagnosis and treatment. The first 50 years of writing in the field of couple psychoanalysis has brought us distinct treatment models, which have opened the door for greater communication and sharing within and between orientations.

Time is troubled for my patient Maya and for me with her. This article describes the nature of the temporal disturbance, as well as the process by which I have come to understand it. Two metaphors help me to define the temporal problems for Maya and for us: music and future vision. Musical dissonance—failures in harmonic expectations, in rhythm and timing, and in responsiveness and temporal direction—provide an analogy for problems between Maya and me. And the collapse of future vision—the projection of a person into an imagined future—is an idea that captures important difficulties in our analytic work.

Theoretical formulations of the castration complex have changed as psychoanalytic theory has developed. A good while ago, Daniel Stern and I were invited to Germany by a large group of movement therapists to help them construct a postmovement treatment interview. Dan and I, along with several hundred attendees, observed a demonstration in which a withdrawn aversive person was induced to join and interact. The leaders then turned to us. Before I could say a word, Dan said “Why talk? You’ve done it.” And I and several hundred others gasped. Subsequently we did help them to construct an interview to provide a verbal narrative that would expand and consolidate the movement story. But I was left with a puzzle: What did Dan’s unexpected, so spontaneous, response mean? On reflection, I realized he was validating the therapeutic power of a nonverbal intervention. And he was opening our minds to why talk; what does talking do? How necessary is it to therapeutic change? What of the other nonverbal forms of communication and the vitality and potential for change inherent in them? These are excellent questions, and in my next several books I included a section on why talk? Nonetheless, something about Dan’s forceful challenge remained bewildering. Consequently, I was delighted to read the reminiscence written by his wife, Nadia Bruschweiler-Stern (2017), about Dan’s early life experience with nonverbal communication with his depressed silent mother and during his hospitalization. Dan knew first-hand, deep in his being, the power, the essential vitality, in narratives told and understood before, and later without, language. He attuned to people’s movements, facial expressions, the music of their lyrics—and in this way experienced vitality intersubjectively. At the same time, the man who asked “why talk?” was a great talker and writer, poetic as Bob Emde writes, and lyrical as Nadia notes. He rendered complexity into understandable words and phrases that, as several authors point out, have become common vocabulary: present moment, implicit relational knowing, moments of meeting, and forms of vitality.

Bonnie Buchele   CONTACT Bonnie J. Buchele, Ph.D. bonniebuchele@gmail.com 411 Nichols Road, Kansas City, MO 64112.

The wary tone that can exist in the relationship between the psychoanalytic world and the group world began with Freud in his paper, “Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego” (Freud, 1921), wherein Freud prefaced his remarks by stating clearly that his knowledge of group life is scant, but then goes on to make two statements that are noteworthy: “The group appears to us as a revival of the primal horde” (p. 123), an observation that evokes caution in the reader because it calls attention to the potentially destructive and regressive forces present in the group. However, Freud also says, “But even the group mind is capable of creative genius in the field of intelligence, as is shown above all by language itself, as well as by folk-song, folklore and the like” (p. 83), a gentle acknowledgement that a group may be capable of “good.” Freud’s comments contained elements of truth then and still do, despite his self-proclaimed ignorance; however, many events occurred in the decades following Freud’s comments that, rather than filling the gaps of knowledge acknowledged by him, have often widened and deepened a chasm between the two modalities and bodies of theoretical knowledge. Growth in the knowledge bases of both fields, bolstered by extensive amounts of clinical practice and good research, places us at a time in history where the guarded aspects of the relationship could be lessened. It may be time for integration based on what we now know about the behavior of human beings. But, first, let’s look at what happened in both worlds.

History of psychoanalysis

Late in the nineteenth century, within the context of Victorian society, Freud, discovering the unconscious life of the individual, was excited about it. Focused there and surrounded by a culture that did not support his ideas, he was far less interested in external factors, forces, and influences. Indeed, followers who expressed interests in external factors and relationships, i.e., Jung, Adler, and Reich, were either expelled from his inner circle or never admitted to it. In Western Europe, clinicians were intrigued by his discovery of the unconscious, as well as this treatment that proved so impactful where other methods were ineffective. Freud visited the USA with much acclaim in 1909, giving his famous lectures at Clark University. Shortly thereafter, in 1911, A. A. Brill founded the New York Psychoanalytic Society in New York City, to be followed in the same year with the founding of The American Psychoanalytic Association in Baltimore (Gifford and Thompson, 2011). Psychoanalysis was launched on its way to becoming the most prestigious treatment within psychiatry; what would later be called the golden age of psychoanalysis had begun.

Bonnie Buchele   CONTACT Bonnie J. Buchele, Ph.D. bonniebuchele@gmail.com 411 Nichols Road, Kansas City, MO 64112.

We have come to a moment in history that may be propitious for the relationship between psychoanalysis and the group world, and could include increased cross-fertilization and enrichment. Psychoanalysis has moved away from its singular focus on and prizing of the intrapsychic functioning of the individual, as was the case with Freud and then ego psychology. With the emergence of the relational theories, psychoanalysts have broadened their interest to how two persons effect one another, one short step away from the smallest of groups: three persons. Neuroscientific findings provided by recent brain research have underscored implicit communication, mirror neurons, and the like—thus shining light on and increasing knowledge about human behavior that has always been part of the group therapist’s theoretical frame. Psychoanalysis is incorporating these findings. As this change becomes part of the common fabric of psychoanalysis, group therapists and theorists may renew their interest in collaborating with psychoanalytic colleagues. These developments may be, in part, why Lichtenberg’s theory has a naturally occurring place for group dynamics and findings within it (personal communication, 2016). If we can move beyond the history and cultivate a spirit of openness within both camps, the time may be here when each community is positioned to be enriched by receiving the knowledge from the other and growing to the benefit of all practitioners and patients.

Estelle Shane and I were inspired to create this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry by a panel organized by Joseph Lichtenberg at the American Psychoanalytic Association: Safety for the Analysand, Safety for the Analyst, Safety for the Dyad (cf. Segalla, 2013). Lichtenberg asked the panelists (Estelle, Arietta Slade, the late James Hansell, and Evelyne Schwaber) to wrestle with the question of what exactly safety is—a feeling, an emotion, or an atmospheric something? He said he views safety as “an aspect of the frame, one that applies to the entire domain of how we interact in an analysis” (Segalla, 2013, p. 993). As Elizabeth Carr and Janna Sandmeyer note in their contribution to this issue, “Exploring the Vicissitudes of Safety and Danger in Psychoanalysis: Developing Trust Through Mutual Engagement,” in a “sometimes fractious psychoanalytic field, the importance of safety is one of the few areas of near consensus” (p. 557).

In the article Lichtenberg contributes to this issue, “Reflections on Safety,” he expands on his question. Safety, he thinks, is an affect and a general state/ambiance that emerges from complex conditions in childhood—a “sense of power as compared to helplessness, the absence or cessation of physical danger and health risk, the acceptance of one’s intentions by another as compared to rejection, the abundance of resources … as compared to their unavailability, and the sense of connection and belonging as compared to isolation and loneliness” (p. 569). Joe then goes on to parse a crucial question: “What lived experiences in the first year of life contribute to a sense of safety, both as a moment-in-time experience of security, and as a general sense that the child (and later the adult) is able to be and do in the world safely?” (p. 569). He finds twelve of these experiences, all emergent in relational experiences with early caregivers. When these experiences go well enough, they provide the “potential of a life-long arc of underlying security, and facilitate the emergence of a sense of safety during an exploratory treatment” (p. 569). The authors in this issue illuminate and wrestle with how analytic treatments unfold when our patients have been unable to find enough of these fortunate childhood experiences1 to develop an internal sense of feeling safe with others.

Safety, or more accurately the feeling of safety and its inverse, danger, is an experiential variable that has received relatively little attention in the psychodynamic literature and discussion. This article attempts to articulate this thinking and some thoughts about bringing the question of safety and danger into the psychoanalytic dialogue.

Forms of Vitality: Their Neural Bases, Their Role in Social Cognition, and the Case of Autism Spectrum Disorder

Vittorio Gallese and Magali Rochat

Magali Rochat

Magali Rochat   Magali J. Rochat is at the IRCCS Institute of Neurological Sciences of Bologna in Italy.

This article focuses on one of the most influential contributions of Daniel Stern: the notion of forms of vitality (FVs). We summarize how fruitful this notion is for social cognition and for the study of its neural bases. We argue that FVs enable one to shed new light on the elements making others’ behavior meaningful to one, thus offering a new take on social cognition. We also show how the notion of FVs can be usefully employed to study the bodily roots of social cognition deficits in individuals affected by the Autism Spectrum Disorder.

I contend that free association, far from being outdated, is a most central feature of the method of psychoanalysis, as it operates an essential reopening of the process of translation/repression. Free association sinks its roots in a Helmholtzian model of the mind and is, therefore, also congruent with modern neuroscience. Bruce Reis PHD

Bruce Reis

Bruce Reis   Bruce Reis, Ph.D., is a member of the Boston Change Process Study Group. This article is in memory of Daniel Stern, with whom I was fortunate to have shared an experience of being-with.CONTACT Bruce Reis, Ph.D.bruce.reis@nyu.edu 205 East 16th Street, Suite 2C, New York, NY 10003.

This article introduces the conception of being-with, which arose from the work of Daniel Stern in infant observation, and is beginning to make its way into the discourses of clinical psychoanalysis. After reviewing Stern’s introduction of the term, I establish that within philosophy there exists strong support for this conception from phenomenological thinkers that promises to ground new approaches to the clinical situation. At its most elemental level, the idea of being-with has to do with one’s embodiment, with a basic constitutional element of one’s humanity, and with issues philosophers refer to as having to do with the condition of being. Several psychoanalytic uses of being-with are then reviewed, all of which reflect Stern’s uncanny sensitivity to the importance and the variety of ways of being-with others.

Analysts use many different methods and therapeutic tools to understand the associations and struggles of their patients. This article suggests that, in addition to other matters we pay attention to for this purpose, it is useful for analysts to also pay attention to physical sensations that they might experience either during a session, or at other times when they are thinking about their work with the patient. I believe that the analyst’s solid familiarity with her own life history and conflicts, helps the analyst understand why her body experienced particular sensations when it did, and what, if anything, this adds to her understanding of her patient. Such understanding can then be shared with the patient, to deepen and enhance the analytic work. I also caution against a casual misuse of such a process.

I find the term castration anxiety a still relevant and important key body fearful fantasy in males, especially expressing fear of the father; as is female castration anxiety an equivalent key fear of the ablation of the sexual and reproductive organs of females, especially by the avenging mother. Freud’s and his followers’ version of the female anxiety, however, has repetitively been shown to be askew since the 1930s, yet it keeps appearing again, as if still worthy of serious argument. To demonstrate its utter blindness to an emotional or imaginative appreciation of female body reproductive functioning, a detailed critique is offered of the once classic paper, “The Body as Phallus” by Bertram Lewin (1933). This article joins in contemporary psychoanalysis’ ever-expanding conversation about the “something more” than spoken language that has long been privileged in our profession. Specifically, the notion is explored that infant research’s conceptualization of mind as dialogic in origin—that we are prewired from birth to participate in nonverbal, affective communication—is consistent with the position that an embodied, dialogic, co-created, empathic connectedness can evolve with severely traumatized, frozen patients whose experience is not just unformulated but unspeakable. This is illustrated with an in-depth account of a challenging therapeutic journey with a highly intelligent man whose social relatedness hid a world of frozen grief and terror of violation. It was only when the therapist could connect with trauma-generated aspects of herself that had remained frozen, could she find an empathic way of being-with and ultimately understanding her patient’s wordless, frozen world.

The evolution of couple psychoanalysis in the United Kingdom is historically rooted in, and currently supported by, what might be called the Tavistock tradition, which principally derives from the work of Tavistock Relationships, a London-based organization combining clinical practice, training, and research. Practitioners working within this tradition draw on a range of psychoanalytic theories and differ in the ways they are applied in clinical practice and with different client groups, but they are united by their focus on relationship dynamics and how these can be affected by unconscious processes. This article charts how the main ideas and practices associated with the Tavistock tradition of couple psychoanalysis came into being, describes the conceptual building blocks that provide the platform for current training and practice, and identifies nodal points that might indicate directions of growth in the future.

Howard Levine MD

Howard Levine

Howard Levine   Howard B. He is a former member of the Board of Directors of the IPA, on the Editorial Board of the IJP and Psychoanalytic Inquiry and in private practice in Brookline, Massachusetts.CONTACT Howard B. Levine, M.D.hblevine@aol.com 1318 Beacon Street, #8, Brookline, MA 02446.

Castration, castration anxiety, and the castration complex were once core, fundamental concepts in psychoanalysis. Have they remained so over the years? What is their current place in analytic theory and practice? From the inception of psychoanalysis, the concept of castration has been intimately connected to Freud’s earliest formulations concerning infantile sexuality: e.g., the sexual curiosity and wishes of children, phantasies concerning the anatomical sex difference, the primal scene and how babies are made, etc. In relation to the Oedipus complex, which Freud thought was the universal nuclear complex of child development and held a formative place in the structuring and development of the psyche, castration fears (fears of the father) in the boy were thought to bring the Oedipal phase to its end, solidifying the internalization of the super ego and ushering in a period of latency. In the girl, recognition of the anatomical sex difference (castration) was believed to initiate the Oedipal period. The melancholic acceptance that she would never obtain the much sought after phallus was thought to conclude a period of mourning, sublimation, and displacement that eventually resulted in a wish for a male partner and a baby (each in its own way a symbol of and heir to the father’s penis).

But that was then, this is now. As reflected in the articles in this issue, there has been an expansion and revision of psychoanalytic thinking brought about by pregenital studies, object relations, feminism, self psychology, queer theory, relational perspectives, attachment theory and many other contemporary additions, trends, and emendations. What then, is one to make of the current status of castration anxiety and the castration complex in the contemporary analytic scene? Given, for example, the diminution—and even abandonment—of the role of drives in the theorizing of many American psychoanalysts, do these concepts still occupy a central role in analytic thinking and practice?

For Freud, at least at a certain critical period of his thinking and probably throughout his lifetime, the Castration complex was assumed to be a concrete and significant fact linked to the problem of the anatomical sex difference and how it was construed, thought about, and made sense of by the infantile mind (anatomy is destiny). First described by Freud in 1908, the Castration complex was associated with the sexual theories of children “produced in response to the child’s puzzlement over the anatomical difference between the sexes (presence or absence of the penis): the child attributes this difference to the fact of the girl’s penis having been cut off” (Laplanche and Pontalis, 1973, p. 56).

The number of women holding elite-level positions in politics and business have significantly increased in recent years, but the lack of parity between the genders is still apparent. This article addresses the stereotypical thinking and the double-bind dilemma women face in obtaining promotions to top positions. It posits internal obstacles that stem from early socialization and may be worked through therapeutically. It proposes that individual psychoanalytic psychotherapy, in the context of object relations and attachment theories, combined with group therapy can facilitate intrapsychic growth towards leadership. Participation in a time-limited group for women may further their insight into the underlying barriers to top positions and facilitate the learning of how to move from fitting in to having a voice and becoming more independent and assertive. Women cracking the glass ceiling may contribute to external societal changes as the relational style of women will continue to gain momentum and redefine leadership in the workplace. Clinical examples will illustrate the therapeutic interventions.

In this special issue on couple psychoanalysis, seven well-known writers within the psychoanalytic literature are brought together to comment on a systematic review of journal articles published over the past fifty years on the topic of couple psychoanalysis. This systematic review provides an overview of writing in journals relating to couple psychoanalysis and delineates the major ideas put forth by authors representing four primary theoretical schools, Classical, Object Relations, Self Psychology and Intersubjectivity, and Relational.

Contributors were chosen based on a primary identification with a theoretical school, having made a significant contribution to the literature and to education within their area. All seven authors, representing the four primary theoretical orientations, agreed readily to collaborating on this issue and set about their task. The task included two primary objectives. The first objective was that authors were requested to read the systematic review of couple psychoanalysis articles and to reflect, from within their own perspective, on the findings. The second objective was to bring their own history, knowledge and expertise to bear on an expansion of our understanding of couple psychoanalysis from within their own theoretical frame. It was suggested that authors might provide further historical background, to share foundational readings that might not have been included in the review due to not fitting into the inclusion criteria, and to reflect on their impressions about the evolution of the field over their careers.

Within this issue, our seven writers, each responding from within their own tradition, have provided rich and nuanced commentary on the findings of this systematic review, as well as expanding upon these findings by providing a detailed discussion of theoretical advances within the theoretical school from which they are responding. Sarah Fels Usher (Classical Psychoanalysis, Canada) notes, “To my knowledge, there are no analysts who work with couples in a purely classical manner, although I would venture to say that most analysts who do couples therapy make use of the concepts born in classical theory” (this issue, p. 359). However, she does go on to describe key theoretical concepts within the classical perspective, how these might be applied to couple work, and how inclusion of these concepts might benefit the work of clinicians working with couples. Chris Clulow, Leezah Hertzmann, and Viveka Nyberg (Object Relations, United Kingdom) share with us the evolution of the field of couple psychoanalysis, a field that was inclusive of many disciplines, in post-WWII England. These authors described the important role couple treatments played in addressing complex relational issues and expand upon the review by discussing these theoretical concepts in greater detail as well as adding important references that might be useful resources for clinicians. Jill Savege Scharff (Object Relations, United States) outlines the evolution of the field of object relations couple psychoanalysis from her perspective as an American writer and introduces the reader to an international diversity that is not represented in the journal articles included in the systematic review. She deftly reviews the field of object relations couple work by integrating the ideas of many writers outside of the mainstream. She further guides the reader in the direction of relevant resources for readers such as books and chapters not included in the scope of the review, as well as articles that are not explicitly psychoanalytic but that she believes would be of benefit to the clinician. Carla Leone (Self Psychology, United States) poses some interesting questions about what we mean when we talk about couple psychoanalysis and provides insightful critique and elaboration on the various themes identified in the review. She then provides a thorough and invaluable history lesson 329

Epilogue: Fifty Years of Couple Psychoanalysis: An Analysis, Discussion, and Future Directions

Heather MacIntosh Ph.D., C.Psych.

Heather MacIntosh

Heather MacIntosh   Contact Heather B. MacIntosh, Ph.D., C.Psych. heather.macintosh@mcgill.ca School of Social Work, McGill University, 3506 University Avenue, Room 425, Montreal, Quebec, H3A 2A7, Canada.

In this issue examining the history of couple psychoanalysis, seven authors from four different theoretical perspectives have come together to respond to the systematic review of fifty years of peer-reviewed journal articles in the field. Having a common starting point provided a jumping-off point for a diverse and fascinating discussion of couple psychoanalysis, which included the vantage points of Classical, Object Relations, Self Psychological and Intersubjectivity, and Relational writers.

In the spirit of this project, each writer had the opportunity to read all of the articles and provide comments. Some of these comments are distilled here. All of the authors felt that through the process of engaging with the review, reflecting upon their own work and that of their colleagues, and reading the work of the other authors, they expanded their knowledge of the field and became more aware of the many commonalities within and between orientations.

Usher, representing the Classical tradition, notes that the efforts of the writers here have brought couple psychoanalysis firmly out of the psychoanalytic unknown into the psychoanalytic known, making the understanding of how the unconscious affects the dynamics of intimate relationships accessible to all analytically oriented therapists, and making the possibility of working as a psychoanalyst with more than one person at a time an intriguing reality. She also noted that although the writers in this issue espouse different theoretical perspectives, like in individual analysis, our goals for the couples we see, and even our theories, are in no way contradictory. Psychoanalysis involves an acknowledgment of the unconscious. Understanding and utilizing this knowledge in the treatment of couples where two—nay, three—peoples’ unconscious are interacting, allows analytic therapists doing couple work to provide deeper and more lasting change.

Clulow, Hertzmann, and Nyberg note that the review appears to have acted as a catalyst in bringing together other writings on couple psychoanalysis that were beyond the terms of reference of the review, but nevertheless are part of the canvass of couple psychoanalysis. A bit like couple relationships, the field of couple psychoanalysis has both internal and external contexts that are vital to making sense of what happens within them. Unsurprisingly, we all converge on a relational focus, and Clulow et al. indicated that they have a sense that the youthful couple psychoanalysis may help nudge its better-established psychoanalytic parents to take more account of environmental influences, and the contribution of other disciplines, in demonstrating its relevance than it does at present. They further stated that it seemed to their reading that although writers might be using slightly different languages, they continue to address similar, if not the same, phenomena in our work. They went on to suggest that, perhaps, a couple psychoanalysis dictionary to help us cross reference terms and interrogate whether and how they differ from each other could be of benefit and might help us to communicate with each other about these stories, and to help with translation. The collaboration for this special issue may make that form of collaboration a reality in the future. In summary, he suggested that perhaps development comes through the process of establishing thesis and antithesis before synthesizing.

Lothane’s description of the development of free association from Galton’s one-person perspective through Freud’s use of both one- and two-person perspectives is outstanding. He characterizes free association as emphasizing the unconscious communication between both analyst and patient. I agree with his position and my discussion illustrates how both analyst and patient unconsciously prime each other to create the therapeutic process. The process can be lively and dramatic, and Lothane’s understanding of the importance of drama has led him to develop the term dramatology to describe the ongoing therapeutic drama that is created in psychoanalysis and psychotherapy as part of this unconscious communication of feeling. The concept of free association continues to develop through these new concepts of how the communication of feeling and knowledge take place unconsciously. I then suggest an even larger field of influence of both patient and analyst that includes unconscious communication of uncanny knowledge that will at times create anomalous experiences. The crucial factor for a good outcome seems to be the depth of the emotional engagement between patient and analyst.

Exploring the Vicissitudes of Safety and Danger in Psychoanalysis: Developing Trust Through Mutual Engagement

Elizabeth Carr A.P.R.N., M.S.N., B.C., and Janna Sandmeyer PHD

Janna Sandmeyer

Janna Sandmeyer   Janna Sandmeyer, Ph.D., is the Chair of the Contemporary Approaches to Psychodynamic Psychotherapy program at the Institute of Contemporary Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis, where she is also the Chair of the Sexual Diversity Task Force. She serves on the Editorial Board of Psychoanalytic Inquiry and is a reviewer/contributor for Psychoanalysis, Self and Context. She is faculty and supervisor at the Washington School of Psychiatry and maintains a private practice in Washington, D.C.

One of the essential features of a therapeutic change process is the ability to establish, within the therapeutic relationship, a sense of safety from which patients can engage and explore the many issues that bring them into therapy. Efforts to gain our patients’ trust so that they feel safe enough to expose their vulnerabilities and engage in a healing process remain at the center of the analytic enterprise, no matter the theoretical position of the therapist. In fact, in an otherwise diverse and sometimes fractious psychoanalytic field, the importance of safety is one of the few areas of near consensus. In our approach, we acknowledge the intersubjective nature of all relational experience and appreciate the powerful processes of mutual influence that reverberate between the analytic couple. As we see it, clinical engagement requires both partners to take risks, tolerate a sense of danger, learn to trust each other, and seek emotional safety through connection and understanding. In this article, we explore a number of perspectives related to building and restoring a shared sense of safety despite what we consider to be the necessary, inherent dangers of psychoanalytic engagement. We include two clinical vignettes that elaborate our views more fully.
